strengths: Clear and well-motivated two-stage framework that decouples behavior learning from planning-principle alignment by combining autoregressive motion-token pretraining with GRPO fine-tuning.
The dual-model rollout design, with a frozen reactive world model for surrounding agents and a trainable ego policy, is reasonable and supports interaction-aware closed-loop planning.
Experiments on nuPlan across Val14, Test14-random, and Test14-hard under non-reactive and reactive settings show meaningful reactive closed-loop improvements, especially without post-processing.
Ablations on fine-tuning, KL regularization weight, and pass@k provide useful evidence that RL fine-tuning improves safety, feasibility, and multi-sample reliability.
Rule-based rewards are interpretable, avoid costly preference annotation, and align with domain planning principles such as collision avoidance, drivable-area compliance, speed limits, and comfort.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: autoregressive motion-token planning and RL fine-tuning with rule-based rewards are both established; the main contribution is the GRPO-based combination, which is incremental relative to concurrent RLHF/RL planning work such as TrajHF and Gen-Drive.

SOTA claims are overstated. Plan-R1 is not uniformly best in the tables, especially under non-reactive or post-processed settings where Diffusion Planner and PLUTO* outperform it on Test14-hard; the paper should qualify its claims.

The paper does not empirically compare against closely related RL/RLHF planning methods (e.g., TrajHF, Gen-Drive), leaving unclear whether rule-based GRPO is actually preferable to preference-based or value-based RL for this task.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor and reproducibility details: no confidence intervals or significance tests across benchmark splits, no code/model release statement, and reward implementation/hyperparameters are deferred to an unseen appendix.

The safety and feasibility claims are supported only empirically through reward shaping; there is no inference-time hard constraint or formal guarantee, so violations could still occur despite improved benchmark scores.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and addresses an important problem: safe and feasible trajectory planning for autonomous driving.
It formulates planning as autoregressive motion-token prediction and combines it with GRPO-based fine-tuning using rule-based rewards, which is a coherent two-stage framework.
Experiments use the nuPlan closed-loop benchmark, including non-reactive and reactive settings, multiple splits, and several recent baselines.
Qualitative examples and the fine-tuning ablation provide some evidence that RL fine-tuning can reduce inherited unsafe behaviors such as speeding, off-road driving, and collisions.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and incremental: autoregressive motion-token pretraining for trajectories has been explored in prior work (e.g., MotionLM, Trajeglish, SMART), and RL/RLHF fine-tuning for planning has been explored in concurrent work (TrajHF, Gen-Drive). The paper mainly combines these ideas with rule-based rewards.

The central SOTA claim is not fully supported. With post-processing, Plan-R1* is worse than Diffusion Planner* on Test14-hard reactive (80.97 vs 82.00) and lower on non-reactive Test14-hard/Test14-random; without post-processing, many non-reactive scores are lower than baselines. The paper overstates uniform state-of-the-art performance.

Technical details are underspecified and potentially problematic. The GRPO objective lacks ratio clipping as typically used, and group-relative advantage normalization is undefined when all sampled rewards are zero—a likely case when safety violations zero out rewards. The dual-model rollout also lacks detail on how ego and surrounding-agent generation are separated and whether the frozen world model reacts realistically to out-of-distribution ego actions.

Evaluation is incomplete and lacks statistical rigor: no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; several main metrics are only reported for selected settings; and key ablations are missing, such as reward-component ablations, GRPO vs. PPO, world-model design, and tokenization choices.

Reproducibility is limited. Important training details (model size, compute, reward weights, token vocabulary, hyperparameters) are largely deferred to an unavailable appendix, and no code or model release is mentioned.

The paper makes strong claims such as “significantly” and “state-of-the-art” despite mixed gains, and the pass@k analysis is only qualitative without numerical values. Some figures/captions are incomplete or inconsistent, e.g., Figure 2 caption omits panel (d).

strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated two-stage framework that decouples behavior learning from planning-principle alignment, inspired by LLM pretraining and RLHF.

It combines autoregressive motion-token modeling with GRPO-based fine-tuning using interpretable rule-based rewards, which avoids costly preference data and directly targets safety, feasibility, and comfort.
The dual-model rollout design is conceptually clean: a frozen model predicts reactive surrounding agents while a trainable ego policy is optimized, enabling multi-agent closed-loop RL fine-tuning.

Experiments on nuPlan cover multiple splits and both non-reactive and reactive simulation settings, and show strong gains in reactive closed-loop performance, with notable improvements over the pretrained baseline.
Ablations on fine-tuning, KL regularization, and pass@k provide useful evidence, and qualitative examples illustrate correction of undesirable expert behaviors such as speeding and off-road driving.
The paper is clearly written and well positioned relative to imitation-learning, RL, and motion-token prediction literature.
weaknesses: The method is largely a combination of existing ideas—motion tokenization, autoregressive prediction, GRPO, and rule-based rewards—so the algorithmic novelty is moderate rather than fundamental.

The SOTA claim is somewhat overstated: with post-processing, Plan-R1 is not best on Test14-hard (NR and reactive) and not best on Test14-random NR, with main advantages concentrated in reactive settings.

The paper does not empirically compare against concurrent preference-based RL fine-tuning planners such as TrajHF and Gen-Drive, nor against PPO, so the specific benefit of GRPO and rule-based rewards is not isolated.
Reward design details, weights, and implementation are deferred to the appendix; there is no ablation over individual reward terms, making it unclear which rewards drive the gains.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release is mentioned, and key training details such as compute budget, GRPO hyperparameters, group size, and reward weights are not reported in the main text.
Safety is framed strongly, but the approach provides no formal safety guarantee and does not analyze reward hacking, long-tail failures, or distribution shift in the frozen world model.
Evaluation is limited to nuPlan simulation; no real-world validation, cross-benchmark testing, or statistical significance analysis is provided.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated two-stage framework that decouples behavior learning from principle alignment, addressing undesirable behaviors in expert demonstrations.
Proposes VD-GRPO, a practical modification of GRPO that preserves reward scale differences across groups and improves safety-critical optimization in rare events.
Strong empirical results on the nuPlan benchmark, especially in the more realistic reactive setting, with large gains over strong baselines such as Diffusion Planner.
Comprehensive ablations: rule-based RL fine-tuning, VD-GRPO vs. GRPO, dual-model design, group size, KL weight, scaling constant, pass@k, and individual reward components.
Provides detailed implementation and reward design in the appendix, aiding reproducibility and future work.
weaknesses: The claim that VD-GRPO preserves absolute reward magnitudes is not fully precise: centering still subtracts the group mean, so it preserves only deviations scaled by a fixed constant rather than absolute reward levels. The theoretical justification is largely intuitive and lacks formal analysis.

The frozen pretrained predictor used as a reactive world model is trained only on expert data and may not accurately simulate surrounding-agent reactions to counterfactual ego actions. The GT replay ablation does not fully validate world-model fidelity.
The paper reports no statistical significance, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds for the RL results, which is important because policy-gradient methods can be high-variance.

The state-of-the-art claim is slightly overstated: with rule-based post-processing, Plan-R1* is not best on every metric (e.g., Test14-hard R-CLS and Test14-random NR-CLS are slightly below Diffusion Planner*).
The token-level adaptation of GRPO is somewhat heuristic and not fully justified relative to standard sequence-level GRPO; additional analysis or ablation would strengthen it.
No code release or broader ethical/safety deployment discussion is provided, though the method is safety-critical autonomous driving.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem in autonomous driving: safe and feasible trajectory planning with explicit rule alignment.
The two-stage decoupling of behavior learning and principle alignment is conceptually reasonable and clearly presented.
The dual-model rollout design using a frozen pretrained predictor as a reactive world model is sensible, and the ablation shows it outperforms GT replay.
The rule-based reward design avoids expensive preference data and includes interpretable safety and comfort terms.
Experiments on nuPlan include many baselines and show strong improvements in the reactive closed-loop setting.
The paper provides useful ablations on reward components, group size, KL weight, and scaling constant.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic contribution, VD-GRPO, is incremental: it is essentially Dr.GRPO (centering without per-group standard deviation) plus a fixed global scaling constant. A global constant scale can largely be absorbed by the learning rate, yet there is no direct comparison to Dr.GRPO, PPO, or DAPO.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim is overstated. With post-processing, Plan-R1* is not best on all splits; for example, Diffusion Planner* achieves better Test14-hard reactive and slightly better Test14-random non-reactive scores, so the improvement is selective.

The safety reward formulation has a technical flaw: per-step rewards are multiplied by safety indicators, but a collision at step t only makes R(y_t)=0. Future rewards R(y_{t+1:F}) can still be positive, so cumulative advantages may still reward trajectories that have already violated safety constraints. Safety violations should terminate or invalidate the whole trajectory horizon.

The main comparison table reports only overall closed-loop scores, not direct safety metrics (collision rate, TTC, drivable-area compliance, speeding) against the baselines. This makes the safety claims harder to verify.

The notation pi_e(y | C, P) suggests conditioning on planning principles, but the architecture does not appear to take P as an explicit input. P is only used through RL rewards, so the formulation is misleading.
No statistical significance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported for the RL fine-tuning or closed-loop evaluations, which is important for RL-based planning results.

The reactive world model is a frozen pretrained predictor and is not validated for realism or robustness under distribution shift. The paper does not show that surrounding agents respond plausibly to the fine-tuned ego policy.
The paper does not empirically compare against preference-based fine-tuning methods such as Gen-Drive or TrajHF, despite positioning rule-based rewards as their replacement.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: safe and feasible trajectory planning for autonomous driving, with a clear motivation to overcome the limitations of pure imitation learning from suboptimal expert data.

The two-stage decoupling of behavior learning and principle alignment is sensible and well motivated. Pre-training a motion predictor and then fine-tuning with rule-based rewards avoids expensive preference data and explicitly targets safety, comfort, and rule compliance.

The dual-model rollout design, with a trainable ego planner and a frozen reactive world model, is effective and well ablated. The ablation shows a substantial improvement over GT replay (90.04 vs. 87.44 R-CLS), supporting the claim that interaction-aware rollouts matter.

The identification of GRPO's limitation in multi-objective planning is interesting: group-wise normalization can erase cross-group reward-scale differences and dilute rare safety-critical signals. The proposed VD-GRPO is simple and directly addresses this issue by using centering with fixed scaling.

The empirical results on nuPlan are strong in reactive settings, with SOTA R-CLS on Val14, Test14-hard, and Test14-random. The qualitative examples showing correction of expert speeding, off-road, and collision behaviors are compelling.

The ablation studies are reasonably thorough, covering rule-based RL fine-tuning, VD-GRPO vs. GRPO, reward components, group size, KL weight, fixed scaling constant, model capacity, and pass@k. These help support the main claims.
weaknesses: The overall novelty is moderate. Two-stage pre-training plus RL fine-tuning has been explored in prior autonomous driving work, and VD-GRPO is a relatively simple modification of GRPO/Dr.GRPO. The paper positions it well, but the core algorithmic contribution may be viewed as incremental for a top-tier AI venue.

The theoretical justification for VD-GRPO is limited. Replacing normalization with centering and fixed scaling is empirically motivated, but there is no formal analysis of why it preserves safety priority under PPO-style clipping, KL regularization, and cumulative token-level advantages. The fixed scaling constant c is heuristic and may not transfer across reward scales.

Evaluation is limited to the nuPlan benchmark. While nuPlan is standard, safety-critical claims would benefit from additional validation on other datasets or closed-loop simulators, and ideally real-world or more diverse reactive settings.

The reproducibility statement is weak: no code release or artifact is mentioned. Although implementation details and hyperparameters are provided, reproducing the RL fine-tuning pipeline, reward computation, and closed-loop rollouts would be nontrivial.

The SOTA claim is somewhat selective. In non-reactive settings, Plan-R1 does not consistently outperform Diffusion Planner, and some gains depend on rule-based post-processing. The strongest results are in reactive settings, so the claim of broad state-of-the-art performance should be framed more carefully.

The dual-model design uses a frozen world model for surrounding agents. This improves stability and avoids destabilizing non-ego behaviors, but it may also limit realism if surrounding-agent reactions should adapt during fine-tuning. The paper does not analyze this trade-off deeply.

The reward design remains hand-crafted and may be susceptible to reward hacking or poor generalization to rare, out-of-distribution scenarios. The paper does not discuss failure modes, safety guarantees, or ethical implications of deploying such a planner in real driving systems.
